title: Design, Fabrication, and Characterization of Bimorph Micromachined Harvester With Asymmetrical PZT Films

sections.heading: Design, Fabrication, and Characterization of Bimorph Micromachined Harvester With Asymmetrical PZT Films
sections.text:
Xiaoxue Dong, Zhiran Yi, Lingchao Kong, Yingwei Tian, Jingquan Liu , and Bin Yang , Member, IEEE

Abstract— This paper presents a high-performance bimorph MEMS cantilever harvester with partially covered asymmetrical functional piezoelectric layers on both sides of a beryllium bronze foil. The optimal PZT coverage length is employed to improve the output power density. The two piezoelectric layers with the controlled different thicknesses for the top and bottom PZT layers can provide three different output powers. Furthermore, a proof mass tungsten bonded at the free end of the cantilever can reduce the resonant frequency. The experimental results showed that the serial-connected bimorph piezoelectric energy harvester can obtain the maximum power density of $2 6 . 9 0 ~ \mathrm { \ m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ at the matched loading resistance of $\mathbf { 6 6 0 ~ k } \Omega$ under $\mathbf { 1 . 5 { \cdot } g }$ acceleration at the resonant frequency of $3 8 . 8 9 \mathrm { ~ H z }$ . The normalized power density of the harvester can reach $3 0 7 . 4 \ : \ : \ : \mu \mathrm { W } { \cdot } \mathbf { g } ^ { - 2 } \ : \ : \cdot \ : \mathrm { \bf ~ c m } ^ { - 3 }$ Meanwhile, the harvester provides good stability under $\mathbf { 1 . 5 { \cdot } g }$ acceleration amplitude.

Index Terms— MEMS, asymmetrical thickness, PZT thick film, bimorph piezoelectric harvester.

sections.heading: I. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
E NERGY harvesting can be defined as scavenging wasteenergy into available energy in the environment, which is of great help to environmental protection and global energy shortage [1]–[3]. Meanwhile, it is a promising technology for the self-powered smart sensors or systems [4]–[6]. There has been more attention to microscale solar [7], thermal energy [8], mechanical energy harvesters [9], chemical and biological energy [10], etc. Among all the recyclable ambient energy sources, mechanical vibration energy could be the most promising way because of its abundant existence in ambient, such as human motion, mechanical equipment, and motor vehicle and so forth. Recently, the reported mechanical-toelectrical energy conversion approaches mainly are based on the electromagnetic, piezoelectric, triboelectric, and electrostatic mechanisms [11]–[16]. The piezoelectric effect has been extensively utilized to demonstrate various devices because of its high-power conversion efficiency and simple operating mechanism [17]–[20].

However, there are several challenges for piezoelectric energy harvesters such as weak base excitations with low natural frequency and fragile structures that are susceptible to shock [10]. Therefore, most reports about vibration-based piezoelectric energy harvesters focus on how to obtain low resonant frequency [21], broad bandwidth [22], high output power density [23] and high stability [24]. In view of different materials of piezoelectric energy harvesters, there are mainly $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { Z r } , \mathrm { T i } ) \mathrm { O } _ { 3 }$ (PZT)-based thin films in $\mathrm { P b }$ -based material systems [25] and AlN thin films in non-toxic lead-free material systems [26]. Comparing to AlN thin film, PZT piezoelectric film is preferred because of its high piezoelectric constant and is also a straightforward procedure [27]–[29]. Cantilever beam is the most common structure since it can generate the high average strain for a given input force [30]. Ambient vibrations are coupled to the cantilever mass system through the base of the cantilever, causing the structure to oscillate [31]. Generally, to match the low resonant frequency of the ambient vibration resources, a large proof mass and a flexible supporting layer will be employed [32]. Besides, most of MEMS PEHs adopt silicon as substrates owing to the mature micromachining process. However, the brittleness of silicon greatly limits its application in low-frequency ambient. Furthermore, the metal foil substrate has low stiffness compared with silicon, which is benefit to develop low frequency PEHs [33]. Moreover, to avoid fracture and obtain high stability, metal or polymer materials are usually used to replace silicon-supported substrates [34].

In this paper, a high-performance bimorph MEMS harvester with asymmetrical PZT thick films layout is proposed. The optimal PZT coverage length is obtained by finite element method. The designed MEMS harvester realizes multiple output powers with different matched loading resistances through the top and bottom piezoelectric layers with different thicknesses. The proposed harvester has a high normalized power density at low resonant frequency and good stability which will be applied in IoT to power the devices or systems.

sections.heading: II. DESIGN AND SIMULATION
sections.text:
Figure 1(a) shows the three-dimensional schematic of the proposed asymmetric bimorph piezoelectric MEMS harvester, which includes top and bottom PZT functional layers, a beryllium-bronze layer in the middle and a tungsten proof mass located at the free end of cantilever. The cross-sectional view and top view of the cantilever of the proposed MEMS harvester are shown in Fig. 1(b). The thickness $( t _ { t _ { - } p z t } )$ of top PZT layer is set as $2 5 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ due to the limitation of micromachining process. The thickness $( t _ { b _ { - } p z t } )$ of bottom PZT layer is set as $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . While the thickness $\left( t _ { s u b } \right)$ , width $( w )$ and length $( L )$ of the beryllium-bronze as substrate layer are $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ , $3 \mathrm { m m }$ and $1 8 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively. Meanwhile, the length and height of the tungsten proof mass is $5 \ \mathrm { m m }$ and $0 . 4 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ , respectively.

![](images/020d4819eb048f67b846afe1ae546044d01676b29e2d6684fbabf70f6220e0b1.jpg)  
Fig. 1. (a) Structural schematic of the designed cantilever. (b) The cross-sectional view and top view of the cantilever structure.

The output performances of the harvesters with various PZT film length layouts are simulated by the COMSOL Multiphysical software. To obtain the matched resistance, the resonant frequency of the harvester is obtained under the eigen modes. And the maximum output power density was obtained at the matched loading resistance. The mechanical damping ratio used in the simulation is set as 0.0125. Figure 2 (a) shows the simulated power as a function of resistances from $1 0 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ to $1 \ \mathbf { M } \Omega$ and the varied PZT coverage length changed from $1 \ \mathrm { m m }$ to $1 3 ~ \mathrm { \ m m }$ under $1 . 5 \mathrm { \textrm { g } }$ acceleration amplitude. The simulation results show that the maximum power density performs increasing at the initial stage and then decrease with the PZT coverage length. Therefore, there is an optimal length of PZT thick film for the maximum output power. The bimorph piezoelectric energy harvester with the length of 2, 3 and $4 \mathrm { m m }$ generates 0.25, 0.26 and $0 . 2 5 \mathrm { \ m W }$ power for the matched loading resistance of 2, 1 and $0 . 5 \mathrm { \bf ~ M } \Omega$ , respectively. Their output powers are very close while the matched resistance of the harvester with $4 \mathrm { m m }$ PZT length is the smallest one among them. Additionally, the eigenfrequency increases with the PZT thick film coverage length (Fig. 2(b)). Therefore, $4 \ \mathrm { m m } \ \mathrm { P Z T }$ coverage length is selected to fabricate the harvester because it can match low optimum load resistance and has relatively good output performance.

It is observed that the stress distributes uniformly along the PZT and hence, the piezoelectric material is effectively utilized.

sections.heading: III. FABRICATION PROCESS AND EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
sections.text:
As shown in Figure 4, the manufacturing process of the MEMS energy harvester with partially covered PZT thick film is mainly composed of the following seven steps. The proposed bimorph piezoelectric energy harvester uses the commercial bulk PZT from Fuji Ceramics Corporation as piezoelectric layer since it has high electromechanical coupling factor $( \mathbf { k } _ { 3 1 } = 0 . 3 9 )$ and piezoelectric coefficients $\mathrm { { ( d } } _ { 3 1 } =$ $- 2 1 0 \ \mathrm { p C \ N ^ { - 1 } } ,$ ). First, the surface of the bulk PZT $( 4 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ was polished and the conductive layer $2 0 \mathrm { n m } \mathrm { C r }$ , 180 nm Au) was sputtered on this side. The purpose of polishing is to improve the bonding force. The bulk PZT was cut into two parts using laser cutting machine. Then a beryllium-bronze foil $( 5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ was polished by mechanical chemical polishing on both sides and one side of the beryllium-bronze foil was bonded with the conductive layer of one bulk PZT using epoxy resin. The other side of the beryllium-bronze foil was bonded with the other bulk PZT in the same way. Since the curie temperature of the PZT material is $2 9 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , the bonding was performed at $1 7 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to avoid PZT depolarization for 3.5 hours. Thirdly, the top bulk PZT was thinned down to ${ \sim } 2 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ using mechanical lapping and then polished by mechanical polishing to obtain PZT thick film while the bottom bulk PZT was thinned down to about $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ in the same way. Then the $\mathrm { { C r / A u } }$ $2 0 ~ \mathrm { n m } / 1 8 0 ~ \mathrm { n m }$ ) was sputtered on the top surface of PZT layer as top electrode. The surface of the bottom thinned PZT layer was also sputtered with the $\mathrm { { C r / A u } }$ $2 0 \ \mathrm { n m } / 1 8 0 \ \mathrm { n m } ,$ ) as bottom electrode. Then the predesigned structure with the width of $3 \ \mathrm { m m }$ was formed by the laser cutting process. The additional tungsten block $( 5 \mathrm { m m } \times 3 \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 4 \mathrm { m m } )$ ) as a proof mass was added at the end of cantilever to further reduce the resonant frequency of the harvester to match the low frequency of ambient vibration sources. Finally, the device was installed on PCB plate and the top, middle and bottom electrodes were bonded with gold wires for output electrical signals. ![](images/86064848d350fa2ee9e984665bead2ad95211bc044c2e15676458e67c920d73e.jpg) Fig. 6. The fabricated harvester encapsulated in acrylic shell is shown in Fig. 5(a). Figure 5 (b) shows the cross-sectional scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of the bimorph PZT layers and it can be seen clearly that no obvious holes and scratches occur on the surface of the PZT films. The actual thickness of the top, bottom PZT layer and beryllium bronze layer is $2 6 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ , $5 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ and $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ because of the experiment errors of mechanical lapping and polishing. ![](images/a9ee5553caad65abb7aea597f73883520af0690b269b583c8fec72b8b2184f3f.jpg) Fig. 7. (b) The close-circuit output current under different applied accelerations amplitude. (c) The output power versus the load resistances under upper, lower, and bimorph output modes of the piezoelectric harvester at $1 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ applied accelerations amplitude in experiment and simulation. (d) The average output power as the function of frequency at various accelerations (inset: the maximum output power and power density as a function of the applied acceleration amplitude). The impedance characteristics of the harvester under three different connections (top, bottom and series) were measured by an impedance analyzer (Keysight 4990A). Figure 6 shows the corresponding impedance spectrums and phase-angle curves, which shows the harvester has the resonant frequency of $3 7 . 9 5 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ and the anti-resonant frequency of $3 8 . 1 4 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ in series connection. The optimal impedance is $6 0 0 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . The peak point of the phase-angle curve appears at ${ \sim } 3 8 \ \ \mathrm { \ H z }$ There are similar measurements done between top and middle electrodes and the bottom the middle electrodes. The resonant frequency is $3 8 . 0 1 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ while the anti-resonant frequency is $3 8 . 0 8 \ \mathrm { \ H z }$ in top and middle connection and the resonant frequency is $3 7 . 9 8 \ \mathrm { H z }$ while the anti-resonant frequency is $3 8 . 0 6 \ \mathrm { \ H z }$ in bottom and middle connection. However, the optimal impedance is $3 6 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ in top and middle connection while the optimal impedance is $4 8 3 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ in bottom and middle connection. It can be seen that the resonant and anti-resonant frequencies remain approximately the same while the optimal resistive loads differ from the different thicknesses of top and bottom PZT thick films. The performance of the harvester was characterized by the excited testing platform including a vibration control system, a power amplifier, a shaker, an accelerometer and an oscilloscope. Fig. 7(a) illustrates the open-circuit output voltages at the range of $3 6 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ to $4 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ under the different applied accelerations from $0 . 1 \ \mathrm { g }$ to $1 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ . Based on the experiment results, the output voltages increase with acceleration, and the maximum open-circuit peak to peak voltages reach 9 V, 24.60 V, $3 6 . 4 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ and $4 3 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ at the resonant frequencies of $3 8 . 5 \mathrm { H z } , 3 8 . 7 \mathrm { H z } , 3 8 . 9 \mathrm { H z } ,$ and $3 9 . 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ under applied accelerations of $0 . 1 \mathrm { \textrm { g } }$ , $0 . 5 \mathrm { ~ g ~ }$ , $1 . 0 \ \mathrm { g }$ and $1 . 5 \ \mathrm { \ g }$ , respectively. Fig. 7(b) shows the output currents $( I _ { p } )$ of the harvester as a function of the external loading resistances in series under varied applied accelerations from 0.1 to $1 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ . To figure out the optimum load resistance of the device, the load resistance was connected in series with this fabricated device and varied from $1 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ to $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . The figure shows that under a certain applied acceleration amplitude, the output currents decrease gradually at a range of small load resistances of 1 to $0 . 2 \mathbf { M } \Omega$ and rapidly decreased for the large external resistance. The maximum effective output power can be obtained under the matched load resistances, which can be determined by the equation of $P _ { e f f } = ( I _ { p } ^ { ~ 2 } \cdot R _ { l o a d } ) / 2$ . The output power of the top, bottom and bimorph PZT thick films varies with the external resistances, as shown in Fig. 7(c). The maximum effective output power of top, bottom and bimorph PZT layers of the harvester can respectively reach 0.06, 0.12 and $0 . 2 6 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ at the matched load resistances of around 300, 540 and $6 6 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . However, the simulated results of the maximum effective output power of top, bottom and bimorph PZT layers of the harvester are 0.09, 0.13 and $0 . 2 4 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ at the matched load resistances of around 340, 540 and $6 2 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . Figure 7 (d) shows the average output power of the harvester as the function of excitation frequency at the varied applied accelerations from 0.1 to $1 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ . The inset shows the relationship between the maximum output effective power and the amplitude of the applied acceleration. The bimorph has better performance than two separate PZT layers. The illustration describes that the maximum effective output power density of the harvester has a parabolic relationship with the applied accelerations amplitude. The effective volume of this harvester is around $9 . 6 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ . Thus, the maximum effective power density reaches $2 6 . 9 0 \ \mathrm { \ m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ at $1 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ . ![](images/d2041a6ab1ee9f2f74a1a7e38913e82cb1dfda3444ec72e794a7ebef4cdadaa0.jpg) Fig. 8. To investigate the stability of the MEMS harvester, a high acceleration is applied to evaluate its capability for harsh workload situation. Fig. 8(a) describes the harvester has a stable output voltage during 3 hours at $1 . 5 \mathrm { \textrm { g } }$ . The perfect sine waves were shown in Fig. 8(b) and 8(c) at the beginning and after 3 hours. The presented harvester provides a large power density and normalized power density compared to recently reported harvesters shown in TABLE I. Moreover, this harvester has a low resonant frequency and high output in a small structure. Normalized to the resonant frequency, the power density exceeds all other reports. For the bimorph PZT thick film on beryllium bronze foil, the harvester has a high output power and normalized power density.

sections.heading: IV. CONCLUSION
sections.text: In summary, a high-performance bimorph piezoelectric energy harvester is fabricated with thinned bulk PZT thick film on the flexible beryllium-bronze substrate. Optimal coverage length of piezoelectric layer is effective to enhance its output performance. The harvester with asymmetrical thickness of the PZT thick film provides different output power. Under $1 . 5 \ \mathrm { g }$ acceleration at the frequency of $3 8 . 8 9 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , the experimental results demonstrate that the power density of the fabricated harvester is 6.31, 12.57 and $2 6 . 9 0 ~ \mathrm { m W } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ at the matching resistances of 300, 540 and $6 6 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . Meanwhile, under this excited condition the device can obtain stable output for 3 hours and the maximum output power density is comparable to previous reports.
